question: What are the most common reasons prospects hesitate to buy?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every objection, concern, hesitation, or reason the prospect gives for not buying, delaying a decision, or being reluctant to move forward, including the exact wording or paraphrase, the topic (e.g. price, security, integration, timing, internal approval, competitor), and how OrbitFlow staff responded to it.
assumptions: Question asks for themes across calls, so each call should be read for underlying hesitation statements to be aggregated later

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: It's more than I expected.
findings.context: Price feels higher than expected; the prospect had anchored on Zapier pricing. — Price objection at the first mention of cost, before any ROI discussion. Rachel acknowledges the Zapier comparison is unfair.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: It's a very common anchor. It's also the wrong one, but I'd rather earn that than assert it.
findings.context: Vendor responded to the price anchor by deferring a number until the user model is known, and by challenging the Zapier benchmark. — Vendor response to the price objection.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
findings.context: Prospect needs a clearer ROI case than time savings to justify the cost. — Justification hurdle for budget approval; she would need to replace enough manual work and possibly some Gainsight spend.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit.
findings.context: Prospect fears the tool will become another thing her team must babysit, so the demo may not reflect long-term ownership cost. — Concern about operational burden after purchase, raised by Tom Alvarez.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor. That's the conversation I'll have to win internally.
findings.context: Main internal blocker is whether to expand the existing Workato contract instead of adding a new vendor. — Internal approval and competitor/alternative objection. The prospect says she must win this internally.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
findings.context: The honest comparison is Workato or improving the status quo, not doing nothing. — Alternative objection, reinforcing the Workato threat. Vendor accepted defining the pilot against the alternative and allowed that OrbitFlow might lose.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Prospect worries that approver-only users could force costly full seats, and wants licensing made explicit. — Per-seat licensing concern. Vendor committed to an itemised proposal and did not give a number yet.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true.
findings.context: Headcount-reduction framing would not survive internal finance scrutiny, so the ROI case must rest on consistency and speed. — Internal approval and ROI concern, with the CFO as the blocker.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.
findings.context: AI features are not a reason to block the automation purchase, so AI could be scoped out of the pilot if security objects. — Security/AI concern that could delay purchase; vendor offered to disable AI or scope the pilot to deterministic steps.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
findings.context: Security/BAA is a hard gate: without a Business Associate Agreement, the prospect cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information. — Elliot Greene (Security Architect) states the BAA is the gate; OrbitFlow staff (Maya) declines to give a yes on the call and commits to a written legal/compliance position within a week.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: A written position is fine. A verbal "we're working on it" is not.
findings.context: Prospect will not accept a verbal assurance on the BAA; requires a written position. — Security objection handled by OrbitFlow committing to a written answer from legal and compliance.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: The second one. That separation would help a lot, actually. AI is interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation use case over.
findings.context: Concern about AI/LLM data handling was a major hesitation; prospect accepted phase one with AI disabled or scoped out, reviewed on a separate track. — Security concern about what happens to data sent to an LLM provider; OrbitFlow offered to disable AI or scope phase one to deterministic steps.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: That last sentence. Is it in the contract or is it on a marketing page?
findings.context: Prospect wants the contractual commitment that customer workflow content is not used to train shared models, not just marketing claims. — OrbitFlow staff stated the no-training commitment; prospect challenged whether it is contractual.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security tells us whether the BAA requirement can be met. If the answer's no, the price is irrelevant.
findings.context: Pricing is not a near-term discussion; procurement will not engage on price until security confirms the BAA can be met, so price is irrelevant if the answer is no. — Prospect declined to react to Enterprise pricing; OrbitFlow respected it and asked for a user model before quoting.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Prospect is wary of per-seat cost surprises; wants licensing modeled on actual builder and approver population. — Pricing hesitation tied to user definition; OrbitFlow committed to an itemised model rather than a headline number.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Power Automate. Or just improving what we already have. Those are the real competitors, not another workflow vendor.
findings.context: Prospect would not pursue a migration away from Microsoft; Power Automate is already covered by their Microsoft agreement, a procurement concern, and is a real competitor alternative. — Competitor/alternative hesitation; OrbitFlow positioned as complementary for business-owned workflows.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: a successful pilot would not automatically mean we can deploy broadly. Those are two different decisions and they have different approvers.
findings.context: Prospect states a successful pilot does not automatically mean broad deployment; pilot and full deployment have different approvers. — Hesitation about committing beyond a pilot; OrbitFlow acknowledged it.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: No production launch before Q4. That's firm.
findings.context: No production launch before Q4; the prospect has a firm timing constraint, with only a non-sensitive proof of concept possible in August. — Timing constraint on decision; OrbitFlow proposed pilot-first path.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation.
findings.context: Prospect's past experience with an internal tool that teams routed around creates adoption risk; requires adoption measured in the pilot. — Concern about adoption, not price; OrbitFlow agreed to pilot criteria including the change-management scenario.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: We have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without seeing the record contents.
findings.context: Prospect has concerns about field-level data exposure in run logs; requires masking so admins can see step failures without record contents. — Data-access risk; OrbitFlow said masking is a design conversation, not a checkbox.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: In practice it lives or dies on whether the permission model is genuinely least-privilege or just a UI that hides things.
findings.context: Prospect is skeptical of least-privilege claims for the permission model and wants it demonstrated. — Concern about operations-team access; OrbitFlow agreed to demo the permission model.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Good, because I have been burned by the logo page.
findings.context: Prospect is wary of vendor claims about integrations; wants each required operation validated in a pilot rather than trusting a logo page, and is cautious about Databricks being phase one. — Integration hesitation; OrbitFlow agreed to validate operations in the pilot.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
findings.context: Prospect says the Growth price of eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team their size; they had expected roughly eight hundred to a thousand. — Price objection. Vendor acknowledged the gap and did not dispute it.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
findings.context: Prospect's approval threshold is fifteen thousand a year; the Growth price (about 21,600 a year) exceeds it, so the decision must go to the COO and finance director, which slows the process. — Internal approval blocker. Prospect explicitly says it is a slower conversation.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
findings.context: Prospect is not yet convinced the value closes the gap between OrbitFlow and tools they already pay for (Zapier), and is open to concluding the current tools are over-bought. — Value-versus-cost and alternative concern. Budget is named as the biggest risk; keeping Zapier is a real outcome.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership.
findings.context: Prospect names budget as the biggest risk and says the status quo (Zapier with better documentation) could be the right outcome. — Budget objection framed as possibly over-buying.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Maintenance and visibility. The same two things. Make would give me the branching but I'd still have the ownership problem.
findings.context: Prospect's real alternatives are Zapier and Make; their concern with them is maintenance and visibility, and Make would still leave the ownership problem. — Competitor/alternative consideration. Make knowledge sits with one person.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
findings.context: Prospect requires a native, event-driven Shopify trigger and would not be interested in a polling workaround; vendor could not confirm and deferred to a written answer. — Integration concern, unresolved on the call.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I want to understand where customer data actually gets processed.
findings.context: Prospect wants EU data residency and asked where data is processed; vendor said it is only confirmed on Enterprise, which is the more expensive tier. — Security/compliance concern for UK and EU customers.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Ideally something in place by early October, because after that nobody's changing anything until January.
findings.context: Prospect's timing is constrained: they want the cleanup in place by early October before the holiday freeze, so a decision is needed around August. — Timing constraint on decision.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I'm not saying no.
findings.context: Prospect is not saying no but wants more evidence; they'll decide only after the vendor's cost-of-status-quo and rebuild work. — Hesitation rather than rejection; vendor proposed a four-week time-cost log and a rebuild of three automations.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: It's a meaningful discount, not a transformation.
findings.context: Vendor was candid about the price gap, saying an annual prepay gives a meaningful discount but will not halve the price. — Vendor response to price objection.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Because if the deployment architecture doesn't work, the product is irrelevant.
findings.context: Prospect hesitates on deployment architecture: systems not reachable from the public internet; cannot be called over the internet. Vendor response: agent or controlled gateway pattern, to be validated against their environment. — Architecture/connectivity objection raised as the gating concern; Martin says the product is irrelevant if deployment architecture fails. Vendor's answer is conditional and unvalidated.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: that is a co-determination matter and it must go through the works council.
findings.context: Internal approval/works council (Betriebsrat) co-determination may delay the project by about six months if a workflow monitors employee activity. — Internal approval blocker; vendor proposed team-level aggregation as a design answer.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: It's that we discover in month five that a use case requires a process we didn't budget six months for.
findings.context: Prospect's major concern is that a project will hit a process or approval requirement after month five that was not budgeted, causing projects to fail. — Timing/hidden-process risk; vendor agreed to surface these in the session.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review.
findings.context: Prospect is concerned about hidden professional services and premium connector costs surfacing after architecture review. — Pricing/cost objection; vendor committed to itemised pricing with TBD where unknown.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
findings.context: Prospect is concerned about per-seat licensing: occasional approvers may require full seats. — Licence/pricing objection; vendor declined to give a number until user model is defined.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: I do not think a sandbox is the next step.
findings.context: Prospect will not take a sandbox as next step; wants architecture viability proven first because the open question is deployability, not product function. — Hesitation to move to pilot; the reason given is that architecture is the real unknown.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case.
findings.context: Prospect says the decisive blocker is whether SAP and on-premise systems make implementation too heavy for the first use case; MuleSoft plus custom integration is the alternative some will propose. — Integration/competitor-alternative risk; Martin also says he does not think the MuleSoft alternative is a good idea.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: I do not want that review sitting on the critical path of a project whose value comes from something else entirely.
findings.context: Generative AI is excluded from phase one because its added data protection, works council and legal review would sit on the critical path. — Scope/approval objection; vendor agreed and said AI steps are optional, and customer wants contractual no-training commitment.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Procurement last, and slowly.
findings.context: Regional IT and procurement can make implementation impossible or delay it; timing is slow with production realistically early next year. — Timing/approval; Martin says regional IT cannot formally say no but can block implementation.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project.
findings.context: Prospect's primary gates to buying are model risk and auditability; failing them would kill the project regardless of connector breadth. — Hannah names gates as the blocker; she is the most likely person to kill the deal (security/risk objection).

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: If your product puts a language model in a decision path, that model is in scope, and getting something into scope is a nine-month process here.
findings.context: Model risk framework would put any LLM in a decision path in scope, a process taking nine months. — Concern about AI/generative steps triggering model governance; timing objection tied to risk.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint.
findings.context: OrbitFlow admitted AI outputs cannot be enforced as leaf nodes; it is a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. — Vendor response to the model-risk concern; prospect wants it recorded as a known limitation.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Then that's satisfactory, subject to seeing the actual payload schema.
findings.context: Prospect wants audit trail to be genuinely programmatic (SIEM push), not a CSV download; accepts once payload schema is seen. — Auditability objection resolved conditionally.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: If we say this solves the audit finding and it only solves eighty percent of it, we're in a worse position than if we'd said eighty.
findings.context: Prospect's main hesitation is that the current audit finding (exception handling 'not evidenced') is a compliance risk the new tool must fix; the status quo is risky. — Internal pressure driving the purchase, but also a need to avoid overclaiming.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine.
findings.context: Prospect is worried about usage-based overage costs growing in year two, which finance would dislike. — Pricing/cost hesitation; vendor declined to promise a cap before modelling volumes.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: I don't want to find out in year two that every approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Prospect worries about per-seat cost: approval-only users may need full seats. — Licence/seat pricing concern; vendor said it would itemise.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: It wouldn't satisfy the auditor. But it would be proposed, and somebody senior would find it attractive, and we'd spend two months on it.
findings.context: Status-quo alternative (keep scripts and document them better) is a competing option that could stall the purchase for about two months. — Competitor/do-nothing alternative; prospect says it would not satisfy the auditor but could be proposed.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: It's tight but it's real.
findings.context: Tight timeline: vendor decision in August, driven by a remediation programme date; timing is a pressure point. — Timing constraint; the buyer frames the timeline as tight but real.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
findings.context: Prospect is comparing against Tray.io and has concerns about its debugging and retry/idempotency behaviour; Tray is the competitor it would switch from. — Competitor objection; prospect says connector breadth is a tie and debugging is the differentiator.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Then that's the one to design for.
findings.context: Internal event bus (Kafka wrapper) is not reachable from outside the network, an integration blocker needing architecture work. — Integration concern; vendor suggested gateway or webhook pattern.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: That's above what I had in mind.
findings.context: Prospect hesitates on price: Growth package at £1,800/month is above what they had in mind. — Price objection raised by COO after vendor quoted Growth package; vendor responded that it is good value versus what is being replaced.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
findings.context: Prospect cannot sign software contracts above £20,000 without founder approval; annual price of ~£21.5k requires escalation, which is a internal approval blocker. — Internal approval limit is a hard limit; she needs a justification for the founder beyond 'more robust'.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
findings.context: Prospect is paying for 20 unneeded seats on the 30-user package and objects to it. — Seat count objection; vendor deflected by saying the package is fixed and the seats are just a platform cost.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
findings.context: Prospect wants monthly billing or a 10-user start to trial before committing to an annual deal; vendor's monthly answer was uncertain. — Commitment risk; vendor said 'usually fine' and needed manager approval, and was asked to confirm properly.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough for a company that doesn't have an IT team.
findings.context: Prospect questions value versus cheap alternative: may stay with Zapier plus better process discipline, and fears paying for an expensive tool they do not need. — Competitor/alternative consideration (Zapier, ~£2k); prospect says they may well decide against buying. Vendor said they'd be back in 18 months.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We're an agency, Alastair. Nobody's auditing our onboarding process.
findings.context: Prospect is unconvinced by the governance/audit value proposition because the agency does not need audit trails. — Vendor's differentiator (governance, audit trail) did not match buyer need.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: too fragile for multi-step onboarding
findings.context: Prospect concerned that the product may not be reliable enough for multi-step onboarding; Zapier is fragile with branches and human steps. — Complexity concern about current tool; vendor agreed Zapier is limited, but this also raises doubt about OrbitFlow's own robustness.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We don't have a dedicated IT team. At all.
findings.context: Prospect's ops team has no IT staff, which raises concern about complexity and administration. — Resourcing concern; vendor said it is no-code, but the prospect questioned that.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: If it tells me four accounts are overdue and actually it's six, that's worse than nothing.
findings.context: Prospect is skeptical that the AI weekly summary is accurate enough to trust. — Accuracy concern about AI summary feature; vendor did not directly answer.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: that's going to meet resistance from me.
findings.context: Prospect is concerned the product will force standardised onboarding, which conflicts with per-pod customisation. — Process-fit objection; vendor claimed full flexibility.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Because that's actually the question. Not whether they signed.
findings.context: Prospect wants proof the tool actually worked for a comparable customer; vendor's reference story was not verified. — Trust concern; vendor cited a past deal and could not confirm the outcome.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: otherwise we'll build the new process around the old tooling and then we're stuck for another year.
findings.context: Prospect has timing concern: must have the tool running before the September client-services launch or they will be stuck with old tooling. — Timing driver rather than a hesitation; vendor said September was no problem.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I'm not ready to run a sandbox myself, I don't have the time and neither does Ben.
findings.context: Prospect will not run a sandbox themselves due to lack of time, and needs a tailored recorded demo to share internally. — Evaluation-effort hesitation.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: two other vendors we've spoken to had it as an enterprise-only feature and I'd be surprised if you were different.
findings.context: Prospect doubts SSO is included on all plans and suspects it is enterprise-only, a possible security/pricing blocker. — Security concern; vendor said all plans but was not sure.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: written reassurance that our client documents aren't used to train models.
findings.context: Prospect needs written assurance that client documents are not used to train models before proceeding. — Security/data concern; vendor promised a DPA.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us.
findings.context: Power Automate is already embedded, licensed and approved, and OrbitFlow lacks a first-class Dynamics connector, so OrbitFlow must be materially better to justify switching. — Prospect's main reason for reluctance; Jon Bell conceded OrbitFlow does not have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector and proposed a head-to-head benchmark against Power Automate.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
findings.context: Power Automate's favourable licensing is a cost hesitation; the buyer says it matters more than they would like. — Cost objection. Maya Chen said OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price and reframed the case around operational cost.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
findings.context: The licensing model per seat is a deal-breaker risk: several hundred supervisors would need approve/view access, and full seats for them would end the evaluation. — Pricing and seats objection. Maya Chen declined to give a number until builder and approver counts were known and said the approval-only population would be structured differently.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
findings.context: The Microsoft platform team is expected to strongly oppose the product because it is not Microsoft, and it has killed things before. — Internal approval blocker. Formally an influence rather than a veto, but practically it depends on how strongly they object. Maya Chen said next steps must arm the buyer for that conversation.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Budgeting for next fiscal year starts in October, so if anything were to happen it'd be in that cycle.
findings.context: There is no decision this year; the budget cycle starts in October, and the prospect is still in exploration rather than procurement. — Timing hesitation. Carlos Mendes said realistically no decision this year and asked for an architecture and roadmap session before any commercial proposal.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: UK specifically I'd need to confirm rather than assume
findings.context: Preference for UK data residency is an open security and compliance concern; the prospect says it is preferred rather than mandatory because procurement prefers it. — Security objection. Jon Bell said EU residency is available on Enterprise, UK needs confirmation, and he would not say yes to smooth the call. Lucy Hart clarified it is not a regulatory requirement.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: And this is the thing that kills most vendors.
findings.context: Offline and intermittent connectivity is a concern that the prospect says kills most vendors, since real-time push assumptions fail in poor-coverage field sites. — Technical concern raised by the prospect. Jon Bell responded with a sync-event trigger and timeout-as-exception design, plus a planned offline demo.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Meaning the workflow has no write path to the conflicts system, at all, at the permission level. Not "we chose not to build that step."
findings.context: Security constraint: the workflow must have no write path to the conflicts system at the permission level, not merely a design choice; OrbitFlow responded that connections are scoped read-only so workflows cannot write. — Security/permissions concern raised as a hard requirement; vendor responded with least-privilege connection design and recommended standing connection-scope review.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: We do not have a native concept of a matter-level ethical wall that reads your barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. That does not exist.
findings.context: Matter-level information barriers (ethical walls) are a significant unsolved constraint; OrbitFlow admits it has no native ethical-wall enforcement, so barriers change requires ongoing workflow maintenance and phase one must avoid barriered matters. — Real blocker for scope; vendor was candid that the capability does not exist natively. Customer noted barriers change weekly.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: EU is not UK.
findings.context: Data residency: UK residency is a possible gate; customer needs UK specifically, not EU. OrbitFlow could not confirm UK residency on the call. — Compliance hesitation tied to public-sector clients; vendor committed to a written answer within the week.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Whatever the workflow passes between steps is visible in the run record, yes. That's the honest answer and it's the thing you should be worried about.
findings.context: Run history exposes matter data: whatever the workflow passes between steps is visible in the run record, a security concern. Vendor said field-level masking is a design task, not a checkbox. — Security concern about confidentiality of matter data in run logs; vendor agreed it is a real concern beyond encryption.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: we have a retention policy that says certain operational records are deleted at ninety days, and if your floor is above that, we have a problem.
findings.context: Retention floor risk: customer policy deletes certain operational records at ninety days; if the vendor's minimum retention is above that, it is a problem. — Compliance blocker pending vendor's numeric retention floor.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Off. For phase one, off.
findings.context: AI features are a hesitation: customer wants AI disabled entirely in phase one; sponsor wants AI use case later. Vendor confirmed Enterprise can disable AI and restrict models. — Security/risk objection to generative AI; sponsor frames it as phase-one-only and the AI second use case remains open.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: My concern — and I'd say it's the biggest risk to this whole thing — is that our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
findings.context: Integration effort may be disproportionate: no native iManage/Intapp connectors, so integration is API work with ongoing maintenance, and it may cost more than the value of saving about four hours a week. — Biggest risk named by customer security lead; vendor proposed testing it with difficulty ratings and a services estimate against the cost of delayed matter opening.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: native legal-system connectors are limited. In our catalogue, specifically, limited.
findings.context: Vendor-side caution on integration: iManage and Intapp native legal-system connectors are limited, so integration requires working through their APIs and maintenance when APIs change. — OrbitFlow staff acknowledged this gap directly rather than overselling.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: I don't want to recreate our matter-opening process inside a proprietary workflow language and then be unable to leave.
findings.context: Vendor lock-in / portability concern: customer does not want to recreate matter-opening in a proprietary workflow language and be unable to leave; vendor said workflows cannot be run unchanged elsewhere. — Customer reframed to needing data access and documented logic; vendor agreed to make documentation a pilot deliverable.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: The internal development option is real. We have a small team, they're good, and the argument is always "we understand our own systems better than a vendor does."
findings.context: Internal development is a competing alternative: the firm's internal dev team could build instead, and the decision is often driven by governance and capacity rather than cost comparison. — Alternative that customer says appeals to certain people; team already at capacity; vendor said such decisions often go by loudest voice.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: I would not make a business case that assumes use around privileged client content, because that case would be rejected and it would poison the whole thing.
findings.context: Scope and price concern: the customer would not build a business case around privileged client content; they want proof on low-risk operational workflows and want privileged-content use out of scope, not an upsell. Enterprise pricing itself does not worry them. — Commercial hesitation tied to risk scope; vendor agreed to mark privileged content as out of scope.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: If it turns out every partner needs a seat, this is a very short conversation.
findings.context: Licensing ambiguity: customer has few builders and many occasional approvers; if every partner needs a seat, the deal is a very short conversation. — Per-seat pricing concern; vendor declined to give a number without the user split.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: They're not slow to say no. They're slow to say yes.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: Security and risk have veto power, which is Samir and his director.
findings.context: Security/risk veto: security and risk have veto power and can kill deals late when earlier vague answers prove to be a no. — Vendor said security kills about a third of deals in the sector, usually in month four rather than at discovery.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: So I wouldn't treat "no new interface" as an absolute requirement.
findings.context: Customer softened a prior stance: 'no new interface' is no longer an absolute requirement, since a simple approval dashboard might reduce email; this corrects her earlier statement. — Self-correction; earlier she said partners do not want another interface.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: And I'm much more sceptical about generative AI than Eleanor is.
findings.context: Customer is more sceptical about generative AI than the sponsor, and is seeking written confirmation that AI can be disabled in the pack. — Internal disagreement between sponsor and security lead on AI.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: If Salesforce fields are stale, an elegant workflow will still make bad decisions.
findings.context: Prospect's data-quality concern: stale Salesforce fields would make an automated workflow make bad decisions, and health scores are unreliable because fewer than half of CSMs update underlying fields consistently. — Objection to building on existing data; raised by Director of BI, challenging SVP's view that health scores are reliable. OrbitFlow response: weight signals by how they're produced, use machine-generated usage and structured ticket data as inputs, show human-maintained fields as context only.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: If the signal isn't in the data, we can't manufacture it. And I'd rather you found that out with a query than with a pilot.
findings.context: Prospect wants proof the signal exists in historical data before buying; OrbitFlow suggested a backward-looking test using past escalations first. — Hesitation about whether the project should exist at all; OrbitFlow proposed a query-first test to avoid a costly pilot.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Because to measure false positives I need to know which accounts were fine, and "fine" isn't recorded anywhere.
findings.context: Prospect is skeptical that a false-positive rate can be measured because 'fine' accounts are not recorded. — Measurement concern about validating the system; OrbitFlow said this problem applies to any approach including Gainsight.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: the forty-percent thing wasn't a licensing failure, it was an implementation failure.
findings.context: Expanding the existing Gainsight deployment is the main competing alternative; prospect wants a cost comparison including implementation effort. Prior Gainsight rollout only reached about 40% implementation because the owner left. — Competitor objection tied to implementation risk rather than licensing; OrbitFlow agreed to build an honest comparison.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I think the price is reasonable if it lets us consolidate several manual programmes.
findings.context: Prospect concerns about cost: price seen as reasonable only if it consolidates manual programmes, but the spend on Gainsight is questionable and may surface in the cost model. — Price hesitation conditioned on consolidation value; OrbitFlow said it would not quote a figure until seat split is clarified.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
findings.context: Renewal-retention ROI argument relies on a counterfactual that cannot be proven, which finance is sceptical of. — Business-case objection; OrbitFlow proposed time from first signal to first intervention as a measurable leading indicator.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I'd say no if the data doesn't support it.
findings.context: Internal approval risk: BI lead can effectively block, security can block, and finance can delay; BI lead will say no if data does not support it. — Approval gates on the buying decision; pilot timing tied to a late-September decision and an August deadline.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: if we miss November, the next natural point is March.
findings.context: Timing risk: the pilot must start before the November renewal planning cycle or the next natural point is March; term start in early September makes CS unavailable for two weeks. — Calendar-driven deadline; OrbitFlow pushed for fast next step.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Salesforce fields get overwritten, there's no history on most of them.
findings.context: Prospect concern about data history: Salesforce fields are overwritten with no history, so point-in-time backtesting is limited to Snowflake and partly Zendesk. — Limitation on testing; OrbitFlow noted it aligns with excluding human-maintained fields from the flag.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I'm not having business-critical logic that only exists in a web UI.
findings.context: Prospect concern about version control and maintainability: business-critical workflow logic must be reviewable, and the platform is not git and may not offer a true diff. — Governance objection; OrbitFlow acknowledged it is not a git integration and would confirm diff capability.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I want to know that if I get hit by a bus, someone else can pick this up.
findings.context: Prospect concern about key-person dependency: the previous Gainsight owner left and only 40% was implemented, so continuity of the workflow after staff leave is a concern. — Operational-risk hesitation; OrbitFlow said the product only partly addresses it.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Student-level records are subject to specific protections and our position is that they should never leave our warehouse.
findings.context: Security and data-boundary concern: student-level data (FERPA) must never leave the warehouse; some larger districts may require their own questionnaire. — Compliance objection; resolved in principle by defining the Snowflake view with account-level aggregates only, with the vendor security review still required.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: I think most of what you do could be built internally. We have the skills. The question is whether we should.
findings.context: Prospect Ava Sinclair is considering building the workflow internally rather than buying, citing that most of the product could be built in-house and that the question is whether they should. — Build-vs-buy objection; she names Step Functions and Retool Workflows as alternatives. OrbitFlow's Nina Patel acknowledges Retool Workflows is a reasonable comparison.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: Building it is a sprint. Owning it is forever.
findings.context: Prospect's internal objection to buying is that building in-house has been delayed by time, and the sponsor argues ongoing maintenance is the real cost that Ava underestimates. — Marcus Chen frames the internal disagreement; Leo Grant notes building is visible while maintenance is not.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
findings.context: Prospect is concerned that usage-based pricing on workflow runs could make high-volume event processing uneconomic, and that subflow invocations may be billed individually. — Pricing/cost hesitation tied to the event-volume architecture; Nina Patel does not state billing semantics and defers to written answer.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: The base price seems plausible.
findings.context: Prospect's sponsor says the base price seems plausible but questions whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic versus keeping events in AWS. — Pricing hesitation; OrbitFlow's Leo Grant had quoted the Growth tier and noted Enterprise conversation.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: If subflows are billed individually and the economics invert.
findings.context: Prospect states a blocker: if subflows are billed individually the economics invert, and Salesforce API limits are a constraint. — Blocker list; OrbitFlow responded by committing to written answers this week and load-testing against the quota.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: I've also seen teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance and then spend a year maintaining the integration to the platform.
findings.context: Prospect is hesitant because the platform could create a maintenance burden: they have seen teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance then spend a year maintaining the integration. — Maintenance/total-cost objection; Nina Patel recommends testing time consumption over four weeks.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: We have EU customers and a data residency commitment in some contracts. So EU residency is probably the requirement.
findings.context: Prospect's security/compliance requirement of EU data residency may be needed due to contracts, which is a precondition before evaluation. — Security/residency concern; Leo Grant recommends checking before evaluation rather than after.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: Practically, if platform engineering says the architecture is wrong, you're not going to overrule us.
findings.context: Prospect's sponsor says the internal engineering approval process could block the deal; the veto sits with the engineer, not the budget holder. — Internal approval hesitation; Ava says she is the veto, Marcus says he can't overrule platform engineering.

draft.answer: Across all 10 prospect calls, the most recurring hesitations were pricing and seat licensing [C1], security, compliance and AI-data concerns [C2], competing alternatives or build-in-house [C3], and internal approval or veto gates [C4]. Timing constraints [C5], integration and architecture doubts [C6], and ROI or proof of value [C7] also recurred.

claims.text: Price and per-seat licensing fears came up in many calls. Prospects worried that occasional approvers would need full seats: Acme (Rachel Morgan), BrightPath (Priya Shah), DeltaWorks (Anika Bose), Ember (Noah Williams), Greenline (Carlos Mendes, who said it would end the evaluation), and Harbor Legal (Eleanor Brooks). Sticker shock was also stated: Acme ("more than I expected"), Cedar & Finch ($1,800/month vs. an expected $800-1,000) and Fable Media (£1,800/month, and 20 unneeded seats). Others worried about hidden or usage-based costs: DeltaWorks (professional services and premium connectors), Ember (year-two overages), and Juniper (per-event or subflow billing).

Security, compliance and AI/data handling were frequent gates. BrightPath needs a written BAA position; Ember cited model risk and auditability, with LLMs in a decision path in scope of a nine-month process. Harbor Legal raised write-path, run-log exposure, ethical-wall and retention constraints. UK residency was raised at Harbor Legal and Greenline, EU residency at Cedar & Finch and Juniper, and FERPA data boundaries at Inkwell. Several prospects wanted AI disabled or out of phase one (BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Harbor Legal), and BrightPath, Fable and DeltaWorks wanted no-training commitments in writing or in the contract.

Competing alternatives and build-in-house options were stated across calls. Acme (Workato expansion), BrightPath (Power Automate, or improving what they have), Cedar & Finch (keeping Zapier), Fable (Zapier plus process discipline), Greenline (embedded Power Automate and no first-class Dynamics connector), Ember (status quo or Tray.io), Inkwell (expanding Gainsight), Harbor Legal (internal dev) and Juniper (build internally).

Internal approval and veto gates slow or threaten deals. Cedar & Finch ($15k threshold sends it to the COO and finance director) and Fable (£20k limit means founder approval) hit approval limits. DeltaWorks has works council and regional IT/procurement hurdles. Greenline's Microsoft platform team is expected to oppose. Harbor Legal's security and risk teams have veto power. Inkwell's BI lead can block, and Juniper's engineering veto sits with Ava.

Timing constraints were stated: BrightPath has no production launch before Q4, Greenline has no decision this year because budgeting starts in October, and Harbor Legal plans a Q4 PoC with a Q1 decision. Cedar & Finch, Ember and Inkwell have specific calendar deadlines (October, August, November). DeltaWorks fears an unbudgeted process surfacing in month five.

Integration and architecture doubts were raised. DeltaWorks said the product is irrelevant if the deployment architecture fails and would not take a sandbox first. Cedar & Finch needs a native Shopify trigger. Harbor Legal faces limited iManage/Intapp connectors, which OrbitFlow acknowledged, and BrightPath is wary of integration logo pages. Ember has an unreachable internal event bus.

Prospects also doubted ROI or proof of value, and some worried about maintenance and adoption. Acme needs an ROI case beyond time savings, and Inkwell wants proof the signal exists in its data and finds the retention ROI unprovable. BrightPath fears adoption failure. Juniper and Acme worry about maintenance burden, and Fable wants proof from a comparable customer.

not_covered: Counts are provided only for calls with relevant findings (10 of 10), not per theme, so the ranking of themes is qualitative rather than a computed frequency.
Prospect hesitations on non-Prospect call types were not examined.
assumptions: Themes were aggregated from per-call hesitation statements.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price

Inkwell's BI lead can block, and Juniper's engineering veto sits with Ava.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
evidence.context: Prospect's approval threshold is fifteen thousand a year; the Growth price (about 21,600 a year) exceeds it, so the decision must go to the COO and finance director, which slows the process. — Internal approval blocker. Prospect explicitly says it is a slower conversation.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
evidence.context: Prospect cannot sign software contracts above £20,000 without founder approval; annual price of ~£21.5k requires escalation, which is a internal approval blocker. — Internal approval limit is a hard limit; she needs a justification for the founder beyond 'more robust'.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: that is a co-determination matter and it must go through the works council.
evidence.context: Internal approval/works council (Betriebsrat) co-determination may delay the project by about six months if a workflow monitors employee activity. — Internal approval blocker; vendor proposed team-level aggregation as a design answer.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Procurement last, and slowly.
evidence.context: Regional IT and procurement can make implementation impossible or delay it; timing is slow with production realistically early next year. — Timing/approval; Martin says regional IT cannot formally say no but can block implementation.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
evidence.context: The Microsoft platform team is expected to strongly oppose the product because it is not Microsoft, and it has killed things before. — Internal approval blocker. Formally an influence rather than a veto, but practically it depends on how strongly they object. Maya Chen said next steps must arm the buyer for that conversation.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Security and risk have veto power, which is Samir and his director.
evidence.context: Security/risk veto: security and risk have veto power and can kill deals late when earlier vague answers prove to be a no. — Vendor said security kills about a third of deals in the sector, usually in month four rather than at discovery.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: I'd say no if the data doesn't support it.
evidence.context: Internal approval risk: BI lead can effectively block, security can block, and finance can delay; BI lead will say no if data does not support it. — Approval gates on the buying decision; pilot timing tied to a late-September decision and an August deadline.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Practically, if platform engineering says the architecture is wrong, you're not going to overrule us.
evidence.context: Prospect's sponsor says the internal engineering approval process could block the deal; the veto sits with the engineer, not the budget holder. — Internal approval hesitation; Ava says she is the veto, Marcus says he can't overrule platform engineering.

claims.text: Timing constraints were stated: BrightPath has no production launch before Q4, Greenline has no decision this year because budgeting starts in October, and Harbor Legal plans a Q4 PoC with a Q1 decision. Cedar & Finch, Ember and Inkwell have specific calendar deadlines (October, August, November). DeltaWorks fears an unbudgeted process surfacing in month five.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: No production launch before Q4. That's firm.
evidence.context: No production launch before Q4; the prospect has a firm timing constraint, with only a non-sensitive proof of concept possible in August. — Timing constraint on decision; OrbitFlow proposed pilot-first path.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Budgeting for next fiscal year starts in October, so if anything were to happen it'd be in that cycle.
evidence.context: There is no decision this year; the budget cycle starts in October, and the prospect is still in exploration rather than procurement. — Timing hesitation. Carlos Mendes said realistically no decision this year and asked for an architecture and roadmap session before any commercial proposal.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: They're not slow to say no. They're slow to say yes.
evidence.context: Timing and internal approval hesitation: practice groups are slow to say yes, a firm-wide change would fail, so scope to two practice groups; nothing significant happens in December and January is planning, so PoC in Q4 and decision in Q1. — Decision process blocker; practice-group leaders must agree to process change.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Ideally something in place by early October, because after that nobody's changing anything until January.
evidence.context: Prospect's timing is constrained: they want the cleanup in place by early October before the holiday freeze, so a decision is needed around August. — Timing constraint on decision.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: It's tight but it's real.
evidence.context: Tight timeline: vendor decision in August, driven by a remediation programme date; timing is a pressure point. — Timing constraint; the buyer frames the timeline as tight but real.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: if we miss November, the next natural point is March.
evidence.context: Timing risk: the pilot must start before the November renewal planning cycle or the next natural point is March; term start in early September makes CS unavailable for two weeks. — Calendar-driven deadline; OrbitFlow pushed for fast next step.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: It's that we discover in month five that a use case requires a process we didn't budget six months for.
evidence.context: Prospect's major concern is that a project will hit a process or approval requirement after month five that was not budgeted, causing projects to fail. — Timing/hidden-process risk; vendor agreed to surface these in the session.

claims.text: Integration and architecture doubts were raised. DeltaWorks said the product is irrelevant if the deployment architecture fails and would not take a sandbox first. Cedar & Finch needs a native Shopify trigger. Harbor Legal faces limited iManage/Intapp connectors, which OrbitFlow acknowledged, and BrightPath is wary of integration logo pages. Ember has an unreachable internal event bus.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Because if the deployment architecture doesn't work, the product is irrelevant.
evidence.context: Prospect hesitates on deployment architecture: systems not reachable from the public internet; cannot be called over the internet. Vendor response: agent or controlled gateway pattern, to be validated against their environment. — Architecture/connectivity objection raised as the gating concern; Martin says the product is irrelevant if deployment architecture fails. Vendor's answer is conditional and unvalidated.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: I do not think a sandbox is the next step.
evidence.context: Prospect will not take a sandbox as next step; wants architecture viability proven first because the open question is deployability, not product function. — Hesitation to move to pilot; the reason given is that architecture is the real unknown.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
evidence.context: Prospect requires a native, event-driven Shopify trigger and would not be interested in a polling workaround; vendor could not confirm and deferred to a written answer. — Integration concern, unresolved on the call.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: My concern — and I'd say it's the biggest risk to this whole thing — is that our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
evidence.context: Integration effort may be disproportionate: no native iManage/Intapp connectors, so integration is API work with ongoing maintenance, and it may cost more than the value of saving about four hours a week. — Biggest risk named by customer security lead; vendor proposed testing it with difficulty ratings and a services estimate against the cost of delayed matter opening.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: native legal-system connectors are limited. In our catalogue, specifically, limited.
evidence.context: Vendor-side caution on integration: iManage and Intapp native legal-system connectors are limited, so integration requires working through their APIs and maintenance when APIs change. — OrbitFlow staff acknowledged this gap directly rather than overselling.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: Good, because I have been burned by the logo page.
evidence.context: Prospect is wary of vendor claims about integrations; wants each required operation validated in a pilot rather than trusting a logo page, and is cautious about Databricks being phase one. — Integration hesitation; OrbitFlow agreed to validate operations in the pilot.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: Then that's the one to design for.
evidence.context: Internal event bus (Kafka wrapper) is not reachable from outside the network, an integration blocker needing architecture work. — Integration concern; vendor suggested gateway or webhook pattern.

claims.text: Prospects also doubted ROI or proof of value, and some worried about maintenance and adoption. Acme needs an ROI case beyond time savings, and Inkwell wants proof the signal exists in its data and finds the retention ROI unprovable. BrightPath fears adoption failure. Juniper and Acme worry about maintenance burden, and Fable wants proof from a comparable customer.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
evidence.context: Prospect needs a clearer ROI case than time savings to justify the cost. — Justification hurdle for budget approval; she would need to replace enough manual work and possibly some Gainsight spend.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true.
evidence.context: Headcount-reduction framing would not survive internal finance scrutiny, so the ROI case must rest on consistency and speed. — Internal approval and ROI concern, with the CFO as the blocker.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: If the signal isn't in the data, we can't manufacture it. And I'd rather you found that out with a query than with a pilot.
evidence.context: Prospect wants proof the signal exists in historical data before buying; OrbitFlow suggested a backward-looking test using past escalations first. — Hesitation about whether the project should exist at all; OrbitFlow proposed a query-first test to avoid a costly pilot.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
evidence.context: Renewal-retention ROI argument relies on a counterfactual that cannot be proven, which finance is sceptical of. — Business-case objection; OrbitFlow proposed time from first signal to first intervention as a measurable leading indicator.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation.
evidence.context: Prospect's past experience with an internal tool that teams routed around creates adoption risk; requires adoption measured in the pilot. — Concern about adoption, not price; OrbitFlow agreed to pilot criteria including the change-management scenario.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I've also seen teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance and then spend a year maintaining the integration to the platform.
evidence.context: Prospect is hesitant because the platform could create a maintenance burden: they have seen teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance then spend a year maintaining the integration. — Maintenance/total-cost objection; Nina Patel recommends testing time consumption over four weeks.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit.
evidence.context: Prospect fears the tool will become another thing her team must babysit, so the demo may not reflect long-term ownership cost. — Concern about operational burden after purchase, raised by Tom Alvarez.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: Because that's actually the question. Not whether they signed.
evidence.context: Prospect wants proof the tool actually worked for a comparable customer; vendor's reference story was not verified. — Trust concern; vendor cited a past deal and could not confirm the outcome.
